AI & Data Products · LLM and Agentic Products

Agent Autonomy and Consent

On the morning of 11 March 2026, Meher Dsouza, head of AI product at Nishchay Commerce Cloud, opened the overnight incident log to find that the company's returns agent had auto-approved 214 refunds during a flash sale for a fashion retailer client, totalling ₹9.1 lakh, of which an estimated ₹2.6 lakh looked like duplicate claims on the same order. Nothing had broken technically. The agent had done exactly what its permissions allowed. The question sitting on Meher's desk was not a bug ticket — it was a design question nobody at Nishchay had actually decided on purpose: how much should an agent be allowed to do on a merchant's behalf before a human has to say yes, and what, precisely, counts as that merchant having said yes in the first place.

The idea

Agent autonomy is the range of actions a software agent may take without a human approving each one individually, and consent is the mechanism by which a human authorises that range in advance, in the moment, or after the fact. The two ideas are usually discussed together because autonomy without a clear consent mechanism is not delegation — it is just an unmonitored system that happens to work most of the time. The distinction matured out of two older fields colliding: access control from enterprise software, which asks what can this program touch, and informed consent from medicine and law, which asks what does the person on the other end actually understand and agree to. Large language model agents forced the two together because, for the first time, a single system could both decide what to do and then do it, in the same step, at a scale where a human reviewing every action was no longer realistic. The sentence Meher could say in a client meeting without sounding glib is this: the agent's autonomy should never exceed what the affected party has knowingly and specifically agreed the agent may decide.

How it actually works

In practice, granting autonomy is a design decision made along three dimensions, and teams that skip any one of them are the ones who end up with a surprise like Meher's. The first is scope — which category of action is covered (refunds, but not price changes; replies to customers, but not account closures). The second is reversibility — can the action be undone, at what cost, and within what window (a ₹300 refund is trivially reversible; a ₹9 lakh batch of them, once paid out through a payment gateway, is not). The third is blast radius — how many people or how much money a single bad decision can touch before anyone notices, which is a function of both the size of one action and how many the agent can take per hour. Consent, in turn, has to be expressed at a matching level of specificity. A merchant who ticks "enable AI support" at onboarding has given ambient consent to something vague; a merchant who sets "auto-approve refunds under ₹2,000 per order, one per customer per week" has given transactional consent to something precise and auditable. The step teams leave implicit is writing the second version down as an enforceable policy the agent actually checks at runtime, rather than trusting that the first version implied it.

A worked example

Before the incident, nobody at Nishchay had written the ₹2,000 figure down as policy; it was a default an engineer had picked eighteen months earlier when the merchant base was a tenth its current size, and it had simply never been revisited as volume grew. That is the ordinary way these thresholds go wrong — not through a single bad decision, but through an old default quietly becoming load-bearing. Nishchay processes about 1,200 refund requests a day across its merchant base. At the existing ₹2,000 confirmation threshold, roughly 850 requests a day auto-execute and 350 sit in a human review queue, each review costing the support team about ₹18 in agent time. That queue costs Nishchay 350 × ₹18 = ₹6,300 a day. Meher's product lead had proposed simply raising the auto-execute ceiling to ₹5,000 to shrink the queue, reasoning that the agent's overall eval-set accuracy was a reassuring 98.6%. Meher ran the arithmetic before agreeing to anything. Of the 350 queued requests, about 260 fall between ₹2,000 and ₹5,000; only 90 exceed ₹5,000 and would still need a human. Moving those 260 to auto-execute saves 260 × ₹18 = ₹4,680 a day in review cost. But the 98.6% figure was an average across all bands, and Nishchay's own evaluation set, stratified by order value, showed the agent's error rate on the ₹2,000–5,000 band was 3.1%, not 1.4% — larger orders more often involve bundled items, part-returns and prior disputes, exactly the judgment calls the agent handles worst. At 3.1%, 260 auto-executed requests a day would produce about 260 × 0.031 ≈ 8 wrongly approved refunds daily, and at an average wrongful value of ₹3,400 in that band, that is 8 × ₹3,400 = ₹27,200 a day in losses — more than five times the ₹4,680 saved in review cost.

Meher then tested a second design rather than a second threshold: keep the ₹2,000 ceiling for instant auto-execute, but add a "notify and delay" tier from ₹2,000 to ₹5,000, in which the agent acts immediately and logs the action, while the merchant has a four-hour window to cancel before the payout settles. This removes the 260 requests from the live human queue (saving the same ₹4,680) without granting the agent unreviewed final say on the harder band — the merchant, not a support agent, does the checking, and only on the minority of cases that look unusual. The lesson generalises: the variable worth changing was rarely the rupee threshold; it was which kind of consent — confirm-first or notify-and-delay — matched the reversibility of the action.

Nuances a learner must sit with

Autonomy is three dimensions wearing one name

Scope, reversibility and blast radius move independently. An agent can have narrow scope but catastrophic blast radius (a payroll agent that only does one thing, badly, at scale), or wide scope but low stakes (a drafting assistant that touches everything but publishes nothing). Treating "autonomy" as one dial to turn, as Nishchay's team initially did with a single rupee threshold, hides which dimension is actually driving the risk.

Consent is not one checkbox

Standing consent (a blanket authorization set once), transactional consent (approval per action) and ambient consent (implied by continuing to use a product without objecting) carry very different weight, legally and practically. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act treats these differently for personal data; product teams should assume the same logic extends to financial and account actions even where no statute yet names it explicitly.

Permission is not the same question as autonomy

An API scope answers "can the agent technically do this." An autonomy policy answers "may the agent decide to do this without asking." Nishchay's incident happened because the refund API key had broad write access — permission — while nobody had separately encoded a decision-time policy — autonomy — for the flash-sale volume regime.

An eval score is a frequency, not a distribution

98.6% accuracy overall concealed a 3.1% error rate in exactly the band that mattered financially, and said nothing about whether failures cluster in time. Agents tend to fail together during unusual load — a flash sale, a pricing glitch — precisely when a single average number is least informative.

Confirmation fatigue erodes the consent it is meant to protect

Every additional approval prompt trains users to click through faster. Past a point, more manual gates produce less real consent, not more, because nobody reads the fifth dialog of the day. Design for fewer, better-timed checks rather than maximal friction.

Reversibility, not intent, is what makes an error safe

An agent that occasionally reasons badly is tolerable if every action it takes can be unwound cheaply within a defined window. An agent that reasons well almost always but occasionally takes an irreversible action is the more dangerous system, even with a better accuracy score.

The right threshold is not portable

A ₹2,000 ceiling calibrated for a fashion retailer's return patterns says nothing about the right ceiling for a electronics merchant with lower return rates but higher order values. Thresholds must be re-derived from each action's own reversibility and cost of delay, not copied from another product or another client.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

In consumer products, one person consents on their own behalf, usually through an account-level toggle, and the design risk is dark-pattern consent — wording an opt-in so broadly that a user technically agreed to more than they understood. In B2B products like Nishchay's, consent is typically delegated: an admin authorises actions that affect many end users or, as with merchants, many of their customers, which means the autonomy policy needs a named accountable approver and an audit trail suitable for a compliance review, not just a toggle. Marketplaces add a further twist — an agent acting for the buyer can affect the seller, and vice versa, so a policy that reads as reasonable consent from one side can be no consent at all from the other; Nishchay's refund agent needed a policy the merchant agreed to, not only the shopper. Company stage matters too: an early-stage team often grants wide autonomy because volumes are small enough that the blast radius is naturally bounded and mistakes are cheap to notice and fix by hand. As volume grows, the same threshold that was harmless at fifty transactions a day becomes expensive at twelve hundred, which is exactly the trap Meher's team walked into — a limit set once, informally, that nobody revisited as the client base scaled.

Common mistakes

Symptom: users complain about constant approval pop-ups, or worse, stop reading them. Misunderstanding: treating every confirmation click as proof of informed consent. Cheapest diagnostic: measure time-to-click on approval dialogs; sub-second responses mean the prompt is decoration, not consent.

Symptom: an incident where an agent did something large that nobody remembers approving. Misunderstanding: conflating API access with an autonomy decision. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "what is the largest single action this agent can currently take with zero human involvement," and if the honest answer is "whatever the API permits," the policy layer does not exist yet.

Symptom: a headline eval score looks strong, yet production incidents keep recurring. Misunderstanding: reading one aggregate accuracy number as if it describes every operating condition. Cheapest diagnostic: re-cut the same eval set by order value, time-of-day and load regime before trusting the average.

Symptom: legal or compliance blocks an agent launch outright. Misunderstanding: treating autonomy as binary — fully manual or fully automatic — rather than as tiers with different consent mechanisms. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the action can be reversed within a defined window at an acceptable cost; if yes, a notify-and-delay tier usually satisfies the same objection a flat "no" was raised to protect against.

What good looks like

Six weeks later, Nishchay's redesigned policy had three tiers, each with its own consent mechanism rather than one rupee line. Refunds under ₹1,000 auto-execute instantly, because the value and dispute history made them cheap to reverse through the existing chargeback path. Refunds from ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 auto-execute with a four-hour notify-and-delay window that the merchant's own dashboard surfaces prominently, with one-tap cancellation. Anything above ₹5,000 requires a named human approver, logged with their identity, and that log is what compliance reviews during quarterly audits. Error rates are now tracked per tier, not as one blended number, and the tier boundaries are revisited every quarter against fresh eval data rather than left as an engineering default. The policy is jointly owned by product and finance, because the people who bear the cost of a bad refund are not the people who wrote the confirmation logic. Crucially, the merchant who set the original ₹2,000 default was told what had changed and why, in writing, with the arithmetic behind it — because a consent regime that quietly redraws its own boundaries after an incident is no better than the one that never drew them at all.

Closing

Meher rejected the simple fix of raising the auto-execute ceiling and shipped the tiered, notify-and-delay design instead, reporting to the client that review cost would fall by nearly the same amount without handing the agent silent final say over the band where it was demonstrably weakest. The next thing worth studying, she told her team, is how escalation paths are designed — what exactly happens, and to whom, the moment an agent hits the edge of its authorised scope — because a consent policy is only as good as what happens when it is triggered, not just how carefully the threshold was chosen.

Before granting an agent a wider autonomy, ask: is the action reversible within a window I can defend to the person it affects, and does my evaluation data actually describe the conditions under which the agent will be operating when it matters most?
